tagline.text: The scars of the Pacific War on a rock fortress that guarded Manila Bay

location.label: Location
location.text: Corregidor Island, Cavite City, Cavite (mouth of Manila Bay)

items.alt: The 12-inch coastal gun at Battery Hearn
The Pacific War Memorial altar and the Eternal Flame

children.text: This tadpole-shaped island at the mouth of Manila Bay is the fortress where US and Filipino forces held out against the Japanese to the last in
. A tram tour takes you through Malinta Tunnel, massive gun batteries, and ruined barracks; the island is now reached by boat from Mariveles in Bataan.
Corregidor is a small island about
6.5km
long, lying about
3–4km

south off the tip of the Bataan Peninsula at the mouth of Manila Bay. Seen from above it resembles a tadpole, so its wide head is called "Topside," the middle "Middleside," the narrow neck "Bottomside," and the long tail "Tailside." Its commanding position over the sea lanes into Manila meant it held signal stations and fortifications since Spanish times, and under American rule it was armed as a massive coastal fortress called "Fort Mills."
When Japan invaded the Philippines in
December 1941
, Corregidor became the headquarters of the US and Filipino forces. On the night of
March 11, 1942

, General MacArthur slipped off the island by PT boat and made his way via Mindanao to Australia, where he made his famous vow, "I shall return." The remaining troops held out for nearly a month even after Bataan fell on
April 9
, but when Japanese forces landed on the night of
May 5
, General Wainwright surrendered the next day,
, and about 11,000 men were taken prisoner.
On the morning of
February 16, 1945
, the US 503rd Parachute Infantry Regiment dropped onto Topside and the 34th Infantry Regiment landed on the east shore, launching the battle to retake the island. In the fighting, which lasted until
February 26

, only a few dozen of the roughly 6,700 Japanese troops defending the island survived, and Japanese soldiers trapped inside Malinta Tunnel set off explosives that collapsed part of the lateral tunnels. The two battles left the entire island in the ruined state you see today.
Today the whole island is preserved as a war memorial. The Corregidor Foundation (CFI) managed it from
, and since
March 2024

it has been run by the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA), an agency under the Department of Tourism. Mile Long Barracks, its roof blown off and its rebar exposed; Battery Way, where giant 12-inch mortars remain; and Malinta Tunnel, its walls still clearly scarred by bullets, all stand just as they were during the war, and with jungle covering much of the island, the ruins and nature blend into a unique atmosphere.

Strongly recommended for travelers interested in war and modern history, and families who want to give their children a history lesson. A direct ferry once ran from Manila, but access now goes through Mariveles in Bataan province, so it's important to check the latest schedule and book ahead.

The island tour uses vintage tram-style buses to visit the main ruins while a guide narrates. Guides tell vivid stories and anecdotes from the battles, drawing in even those without much interest in history.
This underground fortress bored through Malinta Hill has a main tunnel about
long and
wide, with 24 lateral tunnels branching off on either side. Built in
, it served during the war as a headquarters and a 1,000-bed hospital. On
December 30, 1941
, President Quezon took the oath of office for his second term at the tunnel's west entrance. The roughly
30-minute
light and sound show now runs only for an extra fee when enough people sign up to fill a group, and at times the tunnel is closed altogether, so be sure to check whether it's included when you book.

The 12-inch mortars and the 12-inch coastal guns, which had a range of tens of kilometers, remain in place. Seeing the sheer size of the guns up close drives home just how formidable a fortress this island was. The coastal gun at Battery Hearn could rotate 360 degrees and fire shells about
26km
, and Battery Way still has four mortars made in
These are the ruins of a three-story barracks that once housed officers and enlisted men; its actual length is about
, so it falls short of the mile its name suggests. The skeletal concrete shell speaks to the destructive power of war, and it is one of the island's most striking photo spots.

blocks.title: Pacific War Memorial and the Eternal Flame

children.text: Built by the US government in

, the memorial has an altar, a remembrance space, and a war museum beneath its round dome. The steel sculpture "Eternal Flame" on the hill behind it is an iconic sight of Corregidor. The round opening at the top of the dome is designed so that at noon around
May 6
, the day Corregidor fell, sunlight shines down on the circular marble altar.
From the lighthouse at the island's highest point, a 360-degree view takes in Manila Bay, the Bataan Peninsula, and the distant Cavite coast. It was first lit in
, during the Spanish era, and was rebuilt in the
after being destroyed in the war.

blocks.title: Filipino Heroes Memorial and the Japanese Garden of Peace

children.text: A relief memorial depicting battles from Philippine history stands alongside a peace garden honoring the Japanese war dead, inviting you to look back on the war from several perspectives. The Heroes Memorial on Tailside opened in
, and 14 relief murals depicting struggles throughout Philippine history, from the Battle of Mactan in
to the People Power Revolution of
, surround the park.

blocks.title: Lorcha Dock and the MacArthur statue

children.text: Lorcha Dock on Bottomside, facing the Bataan Peninsula, is where General MacArthur boarded a PT boat and left the island on the night of
March 11, 1942

. A statue of MacArthur with one hand raised stands here along with an "I SHALL RETURN" plaque. Set against the mountains of Bataan across the water, the statue is one of the island's top spots for souvenir photos.

The Mount Samat Shrine has been listed as stopping admission around
and closing on Mondays, so do this route Tuesday through Sunday, paired with the morning tour.
Direct cruises to Corregidor used to depart daily from the Esplanade Seaside Terminal in Pasay City, but the route was suspended after COVID-19, and as of

there is effectively no scheduled ferry from Manila to the island. Most visits now use boats run by tour operators departing from Mariveles, Bataan. Arrangements change often, so always check the latest notices from TIEZA or the tour operator before booking.
TIEZA, which has run the island since
March 2024

, accepts only guided day tours booked through registered tour operators and does not accept independent visits (walk-ins). Operators submit passengers' names and ages to the Coast Guard several days in advance, and Coast Guard personnel check the manifest at departure.
The most common departure point is Villa Carmen Pools and Beach in Mountain View, Mariveles. There is a morning tour (departs
, returns
) and a noon tour (departs
, returns
), and the boat, life jackets, admission, and tram tour are included. Seats are limited, so it is best to book at least
3–5 days
in advance. You can book on the
Villa Carmen Corregidor tour booking site
Villa Carmen's joining tour costs about
US$50
per person and departs only with a minimum of 12 people, while a private tour that charters the whole boat costs

for up to 9 people. Island admission is included, but there is nowhere on the island to buy food or water, so bring a packed lunch and water. Other operators such as Guia del Mar depart from Camaya Point (MAAP pier) in Alas-asin, Mariveles, and some run joining tours only on Saturdays and Sundays.

Some travel agencies also offer ferry tours that go directly to Corregidor from a pier near the CCP (Cultural Center of the Philippines) in Pasay, Manila, on certain dates only. Since this is not a regular route, check the departure date, inclusions, and vessel carefully before booking.
Joining packages that include Manila pickup, round-trip transport to Mariveles, the boat, island admission, and the tram tour cost around
per person. Packages where you join at the Mariveles pier cost about
per person. Whether a packed lunch, the light and sound show, the environmental fee, and travel insurance are included varies by package, so check before booking.

Private tours for small groups and vehicle charters are also available, but the per-person price rises steeply the fewer people there are; a private tour including round-trip transport from Manila runs around
per person for two people.
Buses to Mariveles, Bataan, depart from terminals in Pasay (EDSA) and Cubao in Manila, taking about
3–4 hours
and costing about
one way. To make the tour start time, it's safest to catch the first early-morning bus or arrive in Mariveles the day before and stay overnight. From the Mariveles terminal to the pier is about
10–15 minutes
by tricycle, costing
Genesis runs regular air-conditioned buses to Mariveles from its Pasay and Cubao terminals from early morning until evening, with a one-way fare of about
. Bataan Transit also runs a route to Mariveles. Provincial bus fares per kilometer rose by about 14–16% from
March 14, 2026
, so the
-range fares in older travel blogs no longer apply, and schedules change often, so check the bus company's announcements before you set out.
From Manila via the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX), SCTEX, and the Bataan coastal road to Mariveles takes about
3 hours
(about
170km
). Tolls run about
one way.
From Clark International Airport (CRK) to Mariveles is about
113km
by road, or about
1 hour 40 minutes–2 hours
by car. By public transport, you have to change to a Mariveles-bound bus in San Fernando, Pampanga, so it takes about
3 hours
or more.
If you're flying in on a domestic flight from Cebu or elsewhere in the provinces, choosing a flight into Clark lets you avoid Manila's city traffic.
Getting around the island is basically limited to the tour tram. The ruins are far apart with many hills, so independent walking between them isn't recommended.
The
December–May
dry season is best, and especially
December–March
, when calm seas and cool temperatures make walking the outdoor ruins comfortable.
April–May
is very hot, and the shadeless Topside ruins get strong sun, so a hat and water are essential.
During the
June–October

rainy season, the southwest monsoon roughens the sea and boat service is frequently canceled. When a typhoon warning (tropical cyclone wind signal) is issued, the Philippine Coast Guard bans small vessels from sailing, so keep your schedule flexible during this period.
Timing your visit around historic anniversaries can also be meaningful.
April 9
, "Araw ng Kagitingan" (Day of Valor), a national holiday commemorating the fall of Bataan, sees commemorations both at the Mount Samat Shrine in Bataan and on Corregidor. Around
May 6
, the anniversary of the fall of Corregidor, veteran memorial events are also held.
Daytime temperatures around Manila Bay are about
even in
December–January
and climb to around
in
April–May
, and rainfall peaks in
August
. In any season, the morning tour is cooler than the afternoon one.

You used to be able to stay overnight at the Corregidor Inn on the island and enjoy a night tunnel tour, but the inn closed after Sun Cruises, which ran the hotel and the ferry, went out of business in
May 2020

; staying on the island is no longer possible, so all visits are day trips. If an early-morning start feels like too much, it's best to arrive in Mariveles, Bataan, the day before and stay at a beach resort or small hotel (about
per night). There are also lodging packages tied to resorts affiliated with tour operators.

There are no restaurants or snack stands on the island, so you can't buy food or water there. Choose a tour that includes lunch, or pick up water, snacks, and a packed lunch in Mariveles before departure and eat at the island's designated dining area. Mariveles and the Bataan coastal road have plenty of seafood restaurants, so after the tour you can try grilled fish, shrimp sinigang, and kilawin (raw fish cured in vinegar). Bataan's famous sweet mangoes and dried fish also make good souvenirs.
Villa Carmen Pools and Beach, where the boats depart, is a family-run beach resort with air-conditioned rooms for 2–4 people (from about
US$50

a night) and a swimming pool, making it a convenient place to stay the night before your tour. If you're exploring more of Bataan, you could also stay at the heritage hotel built from relocated Spanish-era mansions at
Las Casas Filipinas de Acuzar
in Bagac, about
1 hour
away by car.
Tours run on set days and weekend slots fill up first. Book at least 1–2 weeks ahead, and reconfirm sailing status the day before departure.
Passport details are often required to confirm a tour booking, so enter your name exactly as it appears on your passport when booking, and bring your passport on the day.
There are no ATMs or snack stands on the island. Tour balances, tricycle fares, and resort charges are often paid in cash, so bring plenty of cash before you set out.
Bring a hat, sunscreen, sunglasses, comfortable sneakers, and at least a liter of water. Most of the ruins sit fully exposed to the sun.
Phone signal is weak or absent in parts of the island. Agree on a meeting time and place with your family in advance.
If you're prone to seasickness, take medication
30 minutes
before boarding. The boat ride is short, but waves run high in the rainy season.
Good photo spots are the ruins of Mile Long Barracks, the Eternal Flame sculpture, and the view of the Bataan Peninsula from the lighthouse.
Sit near the front of the tram if you want to hear the guide's commentary clearly.
Tours departing from Villa Carmen have non-refundable deposits, and the date can be changed only until
96 hours
before the tour. Payment can be made by cash, GCash, bank transfer, and so on. If sailing is canceled because of bad weather such as a typhoon, the schedule is adjusted.
Flying a drone requires prior permission from the tour operator and the relevant authorities. If you plan to film, ask in advance when you book.
Most of the ruins are structurally unstable. Don't go inside buildings marked off-limits or climb onto walls.
Unexploded ordnance may remain on the island, so don't leave the designated paths and go into the jungle. Never touch any metal object you find.
During the rainy season and typhoon period, same-day sailings may be canceled at the Coast Guard's discretion. Check refund and rescheduling policies before booking.
Old information about a "direct Manila ferry" still turns up online, but no such service currently operates. Verify a seller's legitimacy before sending money in advance.
Dehydration and heatstroke can easily set in during the outdoor midday tour, so drink water often and rest in the shade.

The island has only a first-aid station, and the nearest hospital is in Mariveles. If you have a chronic condition, bring your medication, and if you're traveling with older people or anyone with limited mobility, let the operator know when you book so the route can be adjusted.
The direct ferry from Manila remains suspended. Be sure to check the latest sailing announcements for tours departing from Mariveles, Bataan, and book only through an official operator.
About
40 minutes
by car from Mariveles. A giant cross memorial about
tall commemorating the Battle of Bataan, along with a museum.
Looking back across the bay from Corregidor, you can reflect on the history of the war while watching the sunset from Roxas Boulevard.
Downtown Manila. The walled city left in ruins by the
Battle of Manila — pairing it with Corregidor helps piece together the full arc of the Pacific War.
In Bagac, Bataan, about
1 hour
by car from Mariveles. A heritage resort of relocated and restored Spanish-era mansions.
In Taguig, Metro Manila, about
3–4 hours
by car from Mariveles. More than 17,000 American and Filipino soldiers who died in battles such as Bataan and Corregidor rest in this cemetery, a good stop after your tour once you're back in Manila.
